introduction: “How can I describe Thee, after knowing that description is forbidden before Thy presence?” Most of this guide is the Báb at prayer, and nearly every prayer turns on that difficulty: God is beyond any name, praise or love that a creature can offer, yet the heart cannot keep silent, and so the worshipper offers the admission itself. Isaiah’s unclean lips, Job’s hand on his mouth, Solomon’s “how much less this house,” the Qur’án’s seas of ink and Lao Tzu’s unnameable name stand close by; so do the mystics who found that love goes where thought cannot. The readings also speak hard words about worship through names and through any servant, and the confident tradition of prayer is given its voice: the psalmist for whom praise is simply good, Jesus teaching “Our Father” and saying “we know what we worship,” the letter that bids believers come boldly. Feuerbach puts the sceptic’s reading of the same facts.
questions: The Báb asks how he can praise and how he can keep from praising. What does a prayer become when it is made of that question?

“Whoso worshippeth God through any of His attributes or names … hath worshipped naught,” yet Jesus teaches “Our Father” and the Qur’án gives the fairest names. How do the readings themselves go on using names?
The psalms say “praise is comely”; one reading calls proclaiming God’s holiness “an evident sin.” Are these two temperaments, two stages, or two truths?
“All worship Thee according to what Thou hast created in them.” Feuerbach would agree and stop there. What does the Báb add that he would not?
“I draw nigh unto Thee through my acknowledgment that I do not truly love Thee.” Compare the Cloud of Unknowing, Rábi‘a and Spinoza. What kind of love is left when its inadequacy is admitted?

outside.why: “How can I praise Thee, after praise is negated from Thy direction?” Isaiah, at his vision in the temple: woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips.

“How can I call upon Thee with hope after Thou hast removed me from Thy nearness?” Hebrews tells its readers to do it without hesitation: let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace. On what does each rest its way of approaching?
“How shall I not call upon Thee,” when the heart cannot be silent? Jeremiah resolved to speak no more in God’s name, and could not: his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones.

Reason says make no mention of Him; love cannot refrain. Augustine opens his Confessions in the same strait, heaping up names for a God most hidden and most near, and asking what anyone can say who speaks of him.
“I love Thee and worship Thee though I have neither the power nor the knowledge.” The Cloud of Unknowing: by love may he be gotten and holden; but by thought never.

“I know not by what path I may worship Thee.” Jesus, to the woman at the well, speaks with an assurance the Báb’s prayer declines: ye worship ye know not what; we know what we worship. What is the knowledge he claims?
“Here I stand … confessing my powerlessness and shortcoming.” The publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven.

“Thou art He who cannot be glorified by any praise.” Solomon, at the dedication of the house he had built for God: behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house.
No tribute suffices. The Qur’án: if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, were ink, the words of Allah could not be exhausted.

No praise from His loved ones reaches Him, and elsewhere to proclaim His holiness is called “an evident sin.” The psalms never doubt that praise is right: it is good to sing praises unto our God; praise is comely. Can both be prayed by the same person?
“How can I move my lips in remembrance of Thee?” Job, answered out of the whirlwind: behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.

“How then can my remembrance ascend?” Claudius, rising from his knees, knows why his did not: my words fly up, my thoughts remain below. The Báb’s reason is of another kind. Which obstacle to prayer is the more common?
“I have not truly glorified Thee, nor can I ever.” Jesus: when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants.
“I have fled from Thee unto Thee.” The psalmist finds no other direction to flee in: whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
To love the Essence itself is to seek “the impossible.” Plato: the father and maker of all this universe is past finding out; and even if we found him, to tell of him to all men would be impossible.
Created things “described Thee in ways incapable of knowing Thine Essence.” Xenophanes: if oxen and horses had hands, horses would draw the forms of gods like horses, and oxen like oxen.
None can know its reality “as it is in itself.” Moses asks for a name and is given one that declines to describe: I AM THAT I AM.
Attributes are used “to deny imperfections” and not to assert what the mind conceives. Isaiah: to whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
Names are affirmed only to deny that He lacks anything. Lao Tzu: the name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.

In that station “all names are far from the shore of Its Sanctity.” The Qur’án nevertheless hands the worshipper names to use: Allah’s are the fairest names; invoke Him by them. Why pray with names one knows to fall short?
To describe is to venture too far. The Preacher: be not rash with thy mouth; for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.

“Neither does the obedience of created things add to His glory.” Paul at Athens: neither is he worshipped with men’s hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things.

“All worship Thee according to what Thou hast created in them.” Feuerbach read the same fact without the “Thou”: what is worshipped is human nature seen as another; theology is anthropology. What in the Báb’s prayer resists that reading?
“Even detachment, though a form of praise, falls short … I seek naught but utter negation.” Wittgenstein’s last proposition: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.

“I draw nigh unto Thee through my acknowledgment that I do not truly love Thee.” Spinoza reaches a like austerity from the other side: he who loves God cannot endeavour that God should love him in return. Is love of God possible on either account?
“My very existence is pure sin before Him.” Isaiah: we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.
“Existence itself is steeped in sin and cannot indicate God.” Genesis has the Creator look at everything made and call it very good. Is the Báb speaking of the creature’s worth, or of its distance?
To associate a name or attribute with the Essence is to join partners with Him. The Qur’án: glorified be thy Lord, the Lord of Majesty, from that which they attribute unto Him.

Whoever worships through a name or attribute “hath worshipped naught.” Jesus teaches his disciples to begin with a name of the most familiar kind: Our Father which art in heaven. How do the readings on the Manifestation as the way bear on this?

“Whoso turneth unto Him through any of His servants hath not turned unto Him.” In John, Jesus says: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father. The next reading speaks of worship “through the Dawning-Place of Thy Self.” What is the difference between a servant and a dawning-place?
“None worshippeth Thee as beseemeth Thy due.” Paul: we know not what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
“Thou canst not be known except through Thyself.” Julian of Norwich was shown the same about prayer: I am the ground of thy beseeching.
“We are not omniscient … but a rational person can deduce certain matters.” Socrates: I neither know nor think that I know.

“My soul’s inability to know its own true essence is among the most self-evident facts to my soul.” Hume reports the same failure as a philosopher: when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I never can catch myself at any time without a perception.

Some worship for gifts, some out of fear, some out of love. Rábi‘a’s prayer sorts the same motives and asks to be left only the last: if I worship Thee for Thine own sake, withhold not Thine everlasting beauty.
“I behold Thee through Thine own eyes.” Spinoza: the intellectual love of the mind towards God is that very love of God whereby God loves himself.
“The servant can never know Thee.” The psalmist: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
Plotinus will not allow even the name “the Good.” The Rig Veda’s hymn of creation ends in the same reserve: he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.
The fittest praise is to deny every attribute. Confucius, saying he would prefer not to speak: does Heaven speak? The four seasons pursue their courses, and all things are produced.
In true worship “the worshipper and the words of worship are annihilated.” Paul: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
